frictionVectors.title: European Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas while pressing for investment and market access. Algeria retains strong state control but faces pressure to expand exports and attract foreign technology.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border Volatility
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya strains Algeria's southern security perimeter. External military competition in the Sahel complicates Algiers' non-interventionist posture.

frictionVectors.title: External Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor has drawn competing US, European, Chinese, and Gulf interest because of its access to Central African critical minerals. Angola gains infrastructure leverage but risks becoming a transit platform shaped by outside capital.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain central to fiscal stability while Chinese-linked financing and international oil firms retain substantial influence. Production decline and debt-service pressures constrain Luanda's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Export Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Niger-Benin oil export route remains vulnerable to political tension and border restrictions between the two governments. Benin's role as a coastal energy gateway brings revenue but also exposes it to upstream diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Northern Benin faces spillover from militant networks operating across the Sahel. Foreign security assistance and port investment are expanding, creating dependence alongside stronger state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains significant negotiating power through its diamond reserves and state participation, but sales and marketing remain closely tied to De Beers and global demand. A prolonged diamond downturn would weaken fiscal sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported electricity, regional grids, and scarce water limits industrial diversification. New solar and minerals initiatives could improve autonomy but require foreign capital and technical partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation, local processing, and revenue capture from gold while renegotiating the role of foreign operators. This strengthens formal sovereignty but risks reduced investment and production.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Expanded security ties with Russia provide the government an alternative to Western partners but increase dependence on an external military patron. Persistent jihadist violence continues to disrupt mining zones, roads, and state access.

highlights: Mining ambitions constrained by weak governance

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold and nickel prospects attract foreign operators while opaque licensing and limited state capacity restrict Burundi’s ability to capture value. Informal mining remains difficult to regulate.

frictionVectors.title: RWANDA BORDER PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain tense, complicating trade, security coordination, and regional infrastructure connectivity. Burundi’s dependence on external aid and transit routes narrows its negotiating space.

highlights: Tourism and logistics drive external dependence

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde’s Atlantic position gives it strategic value for fisheries enforcement, migration monitoring, and transoceanic logistics. European and U.S. security partnerships strengthen capacity but also increase outside influence over maritime priorities.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Ports, airports, energy, and digital infrastructure rely heavily on foreign capital and concessional finance. Debt management remains the main constraint on fully autonomous development planning.

highlights: Oil, gas, and timber remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, and other foreign firms remain important in oil, mining, timber, and infrastructure projects. Weak transparency and limited local processing reduce Cameroon’s sovereign share of resource value.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE CONFLICT
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts roads, agricultural supply chains, and public investment. Security spending and fragmented territorial control continue to weaken infrastructure sovereignty.

highlights: Russian security partnership shapes the state

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN MINING ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: The government’s security relationship with Russian personnel and associated commercial networks is closely linked to access to gold and diamond opportunities. Weak oversight raises concerns that security dependence is being exchanged for opaque resource concessions.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads, insecurity, and reliance on neighboring transit corridors leave the country vulnerable to external control over trade and aid routes. Limited state reach outside Bangui continues to constrain resource governance.

highlights: Oil finances the state but limits diversification

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenue remains central to public finance, while foreign operators and volatile prices constrain fiscal sovereignty. Refining, pipeline, and export infrastructure keep Chad dependent on external technical and commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Instability along the Sudan and Libya frontiers and pressure from regional insurgencies preserve the importance of foreign military and intelligence relationships. These partnerships provide regime support but limit independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains effective control over Mayotte, making the territorial dispute a central constraint on Comorian sovereignty and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on foreign aid, remittances, and externally financed infrastructure, limiting its ability to set independent development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral supply-chain competition
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and other strategic minerals attract intense Chinese, Western, and regional competition, while weak enforcement limits public capture of value.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict and border interference
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border involvement around the eastern provinces continue to undermine territorial control, mining governance, and infrastructure security.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state remains heavily dependent on oil revenues, exposing national policy and public finances to foreign operators, price volatility, and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, public works, and resource relationships expand connectivity but raise concerns over debt, procurement transparency, and strategic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire is strengthening regulation and processing capacity, but foreign traders and global price-setting still capture substantial value from its cocoa sector.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external partnerships
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and multilateral actors compete for influence in ports, energy, transport, and digital infrastructure, creating leverage as well as investment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military-base dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position at the Bab el-Mandeb through foreign military facilities, but this creates enduring dependence on external security rents and rival power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked port and logistics infrastructure strengthens Djibouti's regional role while exposing the state to debt, refinancing, and strategic-control concerns.

highlights: Gulf and IMF capital deepen leverage

frictionVectors.title: NILE WATER DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian management of the GERD, viewing Nile flows as an existential sovereignty issue. Negotiations remain vulnerable to regional escalation and shifting Sudanese alignments.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCING DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, Gulf investment, and foreign currency support stabilize Egypt but increase outside influence over strategic assets, fiscal policy, and infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The state retains formal control over oil and gas revenues, but declining production and dependence on foreign operators constrain long-term sovereign bargaining power. Infrastructure and fiscal capacity remain exposed to commodity volatility.

frictionVectors.title: GULF AND CHINESE CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: External partners remain important for ports, construction, and energy projects, creating financing leverage while enabling the government to preserve centralized political control.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide scarce foreign exchange but give outside firms significant influence over extraction, logistics, and technical capacity. Transparency and sanctions risks complicate sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA STRATEGIC PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to Yemen and Ethiopia attract competing regional security interests. Port access and military diplomacy could narrow Asmara's room for maneuver despite its strong preference for autonomy.

highlights: South African dependence shapes economic sovereignty
Sugar and textiles anchor vulnerable exports

frictionVectors.title: SOUTH AFRICAN ECONOMIC LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South African trade routes, customs revenue, investment, and electricity interconnections. This limits independent control over supply chains and macroeconomic policy.

frictionVectors.title: EXPORT-PROCESSING FRAGILITY
frictionVectors.details: Textile and sugar industries rely on preferential market access and foreign-owned production networks. Changes in trade preferences or regional logistics could quickly reduce fiscal and employment stability.

highlights: Conflict and debt constrain state capacity

frictionVectors.title: GERD AND NILE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam improves Ethiopia's control over electricity generation and water infrastructure, but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan. Regional distrust raises risks around dam operations and future Nile projects.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, foreign exchange shortages, and reliance on external lenders limit Addis Ababa's freedom to set infrastructure and resource policy independently. Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners compete for influence over transport, energy, and telecommunications.

highlights: Military transition tightens state control over oil and manganese
Libreville seeks diversified partners beyond France

frictionVectors.title: Resource Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional government is reviewing mining, oil, and infrastructure agreements to increase domestic value capture. Tensions with established French and Asian commercial interests could rise as concessions are rebalanced.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Manganese and other exports remain dependent on strategic rail and port infrastructure. Foreign financing and operators retain significant leverage over logistics and export pricing.

highlights: Senegal remains the decisive economic and security partner
Small-state autonomy constrained by aid and port dependence

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for overland trade, energy links, and regional security. Border and transit disruptions can quickly affect food prices, fuel availability, and government revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Maritime Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing fleets and limited enforcement capacity threaten national control over coastal resources. Illegal or opaque licensing remains a persistent sovereignty concern.

highlights: Debt restructuring limits policy space but preserves strategic autonomy
Gold and energy sectors face pressure from illicit extraction

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated mining damages water systems, agricultural land, and state revenue collection. Foreign-backed trading networks and domestic political ties complicate efforts to restore formal control.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt constraints have increased reliance on IMF support and external capital for energy, transport, and digital infrastructure. Accra is seeking diversification while avoiding excessive dependence on any single creditor or investor.

highlights: Junta accelerates bauxite and Simandou-driven resource nationalism
Mining infrastructure is becoming the core strategic battleground

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Foreign Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project offers major state revenue but depends on foreign capital, operators, railways, and port construction. Concession terms and local-content enforcement will determine whether gains translate into durable sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Junta Legitimacy and Contracts
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses mining negotiations to build legitimacy while resisting a rapid return to civilian rule. Political uncertainty raises investor risk and could trigger disputes over permits, taxation, and project timelines.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy exposed to external buyers
Political instability weakens control of ports and maritime resources

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Raw cashew exports provide vital income but leave producers dependent on foreign traders and processors. Limited domestic processing reduces bargaining power and concentrates value outside the country.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Governance
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political crises create openings for foreign commercial networks and illicit trafficking through maritime infrastructure. Fisheries enforcement and port oversight remain especially vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Fiscal Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and large repayments constrain Nairobi's policy space. Public resistance to taxation and austerity complicates efforts to preserve sovereign control over infrastructure and public assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Competition for Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: China, Gulf investors, Western lenders, and regional partners compete for influence over ports, railways, energy, and logistics. Kenya's scrutiny of major foreign-backed concessions reflects growing sensitivity to sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but lock Lesotho into a highly asymmetric bilateral relationship. Construction costs, procurement disputes, and dependence on South African infrastructure limit domestic control over the resource.

frictionVectors.title: Economic Dependence on External Capital
frictionVectors.details: Mining, textiles, remittances, and customs revenues remain vulnerable to outside market and policy decisions. South African commercial dominance and periodic political instability reduce Lesotho's bargaining power.

highlights: Iron Ore Expansion, Limited Local Capture

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Revenue Control
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore projects led by foreign firms remain central to growth, but weak local processing and infrastructure dependence limit Liberia's share of value creation. Contract renegotiation and environmental oversight remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and investors retain significant influence over ports, shipping, and logistics corridors. Liberia's maritime registry generates revenue but leaves the country exposed to external regulatory and commercial pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Control of Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed factions can disrupt production, exports, and central revenue distribution. Foreign energy interests benefit from access while Libya struggles to establish a unified sovereign framework for managing its principal resource.

frictionVectors.title: Turkey-Russia and Regional Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkish security support in western Libya and Russian-linked networks in the east and south entrench external influence. Rival foreign partnerships complicate reunification, border control, and protection of energy corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, Cobalt, and Ilmenite Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining operations linked to foreign investors dominate critical-mineral exports, while Madagascar captures limited downstream value. Fiscal gains are vulnerable to commodity prices, project financing conditions, and concession disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Land, Environment, and Infrastructure Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors, roads, ports, and energy projects generate recurring disputes over land rights, ecological damage, and compensation. Chinese, Australian, European, and regional commercial interests compete for influence around strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting foreign capital for uranium, rare-earth and graphite projects while trying to strengthen licensing and local-benefit rules. Limited state capacity risks leaving the government with weak leverage over operators and export revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Fuel shortages, unreliable electricity and heavy external debt constrain policy autonomy. IMF-backed reforms and creditor negotiations improve macroeconomic discipline but narrow room for independent infrastructure choices.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-State Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are demanding greater state participation and revenue from industrial gold mining, creating recurring tension with foreign operators. Weak transparency and legal uncertainty may deter investment while encouraging politically connected concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security assistance has expanded as relations with France and regional institutions deteriorated. Persistent jihadist violence threatens transport corridors, mining logistics and the government's ability to control resource-producing areas.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project and proposed green-hydrogen investments bring revenue and infrastructure but remain dependent on foreign developers, finance and export markets. Mauritania is trying to secure stronger domestic-content and fiscal terms without slowing project execution.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Corridor Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports depend heavily on the state railway and external buyers, leaving the economy exposed to price cycles and logistics disruption. Expansion plans could improve state leverage, but financing and regional security remain constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to pursue sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while balancing strategic and economic ties with the United Kingdom, United States and India. Any settlement must reconcile Mauritian territorial claims with the military value of Diego Garcia.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Blue-Economy Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is positioning Port Louis as a regional logistics and maritime-services hub amid growing Indian Ocean competition. External investment offers infrastructure gains but requires careful screening to prevent strategic dependence or loss of regulatory control.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is consolidating control over phosphate, fisheries, ports and renewable projects in Western Sahara, while facing continued legal and diplomatic challenges from the Polisario Front and Algeria. Foreign partners must balance commercial access with contested-territory risks.

frictionVectors.title: External Technology and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale renewables, desalination, automotive and port projects strengthen Morocco's strategic autonomy but rely on European, Gulf, Chinese and other external capital and technology. Rabat is diversifying partnerships to preserve bargaining power and avoid alignment with any single bloc.

highlights: Cabo Delgado LNG remains stalled by insecurity
External security and energy capital shape recovery

frictionVectors.title: LNG SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique relies on foreign energy companies and external security support to restart major LNG projects in Cabo Delgado. Insurgent activity and local grievances continue to limit state control over the resource corridor.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE-LED DEBT PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Gas revenues remain delayed while debt, infrastructure costs, and revenue-sharing disputes constrain fiscal sovereignty. Foreign lenders and investors retain substantial leverage over project sequencing.

highlights: Critical minerals and green hydrogen attract strategic capital

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN CONTROL OF NEW ENERGY
frictionVectors.details: International firms and state-backed investors are positioning for dominance in green hydrogen, uranium, lithium, and offshore oil. Namibia is strengthening local-content and ownership frameworks, but domestic financing and technical capacity remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Ports, electricity generation, water supply, and rail capacity may not keep pace with extractive and hydrogen ambitions. Dependence on external infrastructure finance could dilute national bargaining power.

highlights: Junta pushes strategic break with former partners
Oil and uranium sovereignty remain constrained by logistics

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY ALIGNMENT
frictionVectors.details: The military government has reduced Western security cooperation and expanded ties with Russia, trading one form of external dependence for another. Security assistance has not eliminated insurgent pressure or restored reliable control across the territory.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE EXPORT BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Oil exports, uranium production, and mining revenues are vulnerable to sanctions, border disruptions, and dependence on neighboring transport corridors. The state has greater negotiating leverage rhetorically than it currently has infrastructure to exercise.

highlights: Oil-sector reform seeks stronger state and investor discipline
Power and pipeline insecurity erode resource sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: OIL INFRASTRUCTURE INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline theft, sabotage, illegal refining, and militant pressure continue to reduce public capture of hydrocarbon value. International operators remain important, while the state struggles to secure production and enforce environmental obligations.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND FINANCE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, foreign-exchange constraints, and reliance on external capital limit Nigeria's ability to process resources domestically. Large infrastructure and energy projects remain exposed to international lenders, contractors, and currency volatility.

highlights: State-led mineral governance remains highly organized
Regional security posture raises diplomatic and supply-chain risk

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN DRC MINERALS
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces sustained international scrutiny over alleged support for armed actors in eastern DRC and the movement of conflict-linked minerals through regional networks. Diplomatic pressure could affect mineral access, aid relationships, and investment confidence.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control over domestic assets and infrastructure, but its development model depends heavily on foreign aid, concessional finance, and strategic investors. Fiscal autonomy remains vulnerable to shifts in donor and creditor policy.

highlights: Offshore oil remains prospective, not transformative

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Licensing Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe is seeking credible offshore exploration partners while protecting state participation and avoiding dependence on speculative oil revenues. Limited institutional capacity increases exposure to opaque licensing terms.

frictionVectors.title: External Maritime Influence
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, and other partners compete for diplomatic and maritime-security access. The government benefits from diversification but must prevent infrastructure and security cooperation from becoming strategic dependency.

highlights: Oil and gas revenues face delivery risks

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is under pressure to increase domestic value capture from the Sangomar and Greater Tortue Ahmeyim projects without triggering costly disputes with international operators. Production delays, financing terms, and revenue transparency remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stress constrains Dakar's ability to fund strategic infrastructure independently, increasing reliance on multilateral lenders, Gulf capital, China, and European partners. Renegotiation efforts risk slowing transport and energy investment.

highlights: Blue economy remains the sovereignty strategy

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles must balance maritime-security cooperation with India, France, the United States, and China while preserving control over ports, airfields, and exclusive economic zone surveillance. Competition is usually diplomatic but could intensify around dual-use infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Climate Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on tourism and imported fuel limits strategic autonomy, while climate impacts threaten coastal infrastructure and fisheries. External climate finance is essential but can narrow domestic policy space.

highlights: Mining investment expands faster than local capture

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mining Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore operations generate export earnings but leave Sierra Leone exposed to commodity cycles, foreign operators, and disputes over taxation, local procurement, and environmental impacts. Limited processing capacity keeps much of the value chain offshore.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and mining-logistics projects can improve connectivity while creating long-term commercial and political leverage. Freetown faces pressure to secure transparent concessions and prevent strategic infrastructure from being tied to narrow mineral interests.

highlights: Sovereignty contested across land and sea

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Somaliland Competition
frictionVectors.details: The federal government is balancing Turkey, the Gulf states, Egypt, Ethiopia, and Western partners while defending territorial integrity and maritime rights. Port access and competing arrangements with Somaliland and regional powers risk escalating diplomatic and security tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resources and Weak Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore oil and gas assets could strengthen state finances but also intensify disputes over federal-regional authority, licensing, and revenue sharing. Security constraints and limited regulatory capacity leave the sector vulnerable to external capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral investment competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation of platinum, manganese and rare-earth resources while balancing Chinese, Western and Gulf investment. Regulatory uncertainty and infrastructure bottlenecks limit Pretoria's leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Rail, port and electricity strain
frictionVectors.details: Eskom reliability problems and Transnet logistics failures continue to reduce export capacity and weaken sovereign control over strategic supply chains. Public-private concessions may improve performance but increase foreign influence over infrastructure.

highlights: Oil revenue hostage to Sudan war

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence through Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on pipelines and terminals in Sudan, leaving revenue flows exposed to Sudanese conflict, sabotage and political bargaining. Foreign operators and neighboring states retain substantial leverage over production and transit.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector opacity and armed patronage
frictionVectors.details: Production-sharing arrangements, security payments and opaque revenue management allow external firms and domestic elites to capture much of the sector's value. Weak institutions limit the government's ability to convert oil into broad-based sovereignty or development.

highlights: Gold and Red Sea assets draw outside powers

frictionVectors.title: Gold smuggling and external sponsorship
frictionVectors.details: Competing military networks and cross-border traders continue to channel gold outside formal state systems. Gulf, Russian and regional actors pursue access and influence, deepening the link between mineral extraction and wartime finance.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Ports, naval access and transport corridors on the Red Sea remain strategic prizes amid rivalry involving Gulf states, Russia and other external powers. Conflict-related fragmentation makes long-term control of these assets unstable and vulnerable to concessionary deals.

highlights: LNG and corridor projects reshape leverage

frictionVectors.title: Delayed offshore gas development
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is negotiating to retain greater fiscal and local-development benefits from major LNG projects while attracting international capital and technology. Delays and contract uncertainty risk reducing bargaining power against global energy firms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail influence competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed and Gulf-linked infrastructure interests compete with Western and regional partners around Dar es Salaam, Bagamoyo and transport corridors. Tanzania is using this rivalry to diversify options, but debt, concession and access terms require careful management.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade gateway
Phosphate and logistics value face external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and concession politics
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is central to Togo's revenue and regional influence, but foreign operators, lenders and shipping networks shape its commercial autonomy. Competition from other Gulf of Guinea ports could increase pressure for favorable concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector modernization gap
frictionVectors.details: Togo is trying to expand and modernize phosphate production while retaining more value domestically. Financing, technology and export access remain dependent on external partners, limiting the state's ability to fully control the sector.

frictionVectors.title: European Migration Leverage
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains closely tied to Tunisia’s management of migration routes, creating sovereignty concerns over border policy and domestic accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Dependence and Phosphate Decline
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and aging infrastructure, while disruptions in phosphate production weaken one of its few major strategic export sectors.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Transit Risk
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline faces sustained environmental, legal, and financing pressure, while reliance on external partners limits Kampala’s control over project execution and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand national capacity but increase repayment obligations and dependence on foreign contractors, lenders, and operating expertise.

highlights: Copper Sovereignty Returns to Center Stage

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Copper Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking more domestic processing and stronger fiscal returns from copper, but foreign ownership, trading networks, and technology dependence still constrain sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Power Shortages Threaten Mining Control
frictionVectors.details: Electricity deficits and drought-driven hydropower weakness undermine copper production and increase reliance on imported power, emergency generation, and external investment.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Critical-Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is tightening controls on unprocessed mineral exports, but Chinese-linked capital, technology, and offtake arrangements continue to shape the country’s ability to capture value from lithium and other strategic minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, Currency, and Infrastructure Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted financial access complicate investment and infrastructure renewal, while currency instability encourages opaque resource-for-finance arrangements and weakens public oversight.
